posts.title: RIP Ken St. Andre (1947–2026)
posts.description: It's been brought to my attention that Ken St. Andre, creator of Tunnels & Trolls , the second published roleplaying game, has died. That's a great loss for the hobby, as another of the founding generation passes on from this life. Unlike many of the people I've eulogized on this blog over the years, I actually met Ken when he attended OSRCon in Toronto back in 2012 . He even played in my Dwimmermount session at the convention, where his unorthodox style of play caused something of a stir among other attendees. Earlier that same year, I also interviewed him . Consequently, I feel this death a little more keenly than I do the deaths of other greats of our hobby. I'd never say Ken and I were friends , but we knew one another and occasionally exchanged emails. Ken was very much a real person to me. posts.title: Envy
posts.description: At Gamehole Con this year, I was fortunate to have had the opportunity to hang out for extended periods with several notables who work for or with Goodman Games, starting with the Dark Master himself, Joseph Goodman. Joe has long been a fan and supporter of Grognardia and, over the years, he's been kind enough to ask me to do a few small projects for his company, generally introductions or essays that touch on our shared passion for the authors and tales of Appendix N. It's always great to have the chance to catch up with him and hear his stories. Alongside Joe, I also had the distinct pleasure of meeting several other Goodman stalwarts, like Harley Stroh. Harley's name has been known to me for years, long before I even started this blog. I remember seeing his byline on the 3e era Dungeon Crawl Classics adventures and being impressed by his work. posts.title: Too Many
posts.description: Is it possible to have too many dice ? That's a question I recently asked myself after attending Gamehole Con and CleriCon this month. When I was younger, my answer would certainly have been no , in large part because, in the '80s, there weren't that many dice to buy, at least where I grew up. For the longest time, the only dice I ever owned were the ones that came in RPG boxed sets. They were almost universally terrible – either the infamous "low impact" dice associated with the Holmes D&D Basic Set or the almost-as-bad Dragon Dice from other TSR offerings. I think the first decent dice I acquired were the Gamescience set included in Call of Cthulhu , but it's possible I'm misremembering. Regardless, I cherished every set of dice I acquired, even the bad ones, because, as I said, I didn't have the luxury of being able to pick and choose from a vast array of options.
